title: Starch
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: One cup of cassava starch, half a cup of room-temperature water and a teaspoon and a half of palm oil, all into a cool pan together — worked until it is translucent and glassy orange.
longDesc: Starch is the Delta's swallow and it is the most exactly specified recipe in the whole Nigerian record: one cup of starch, half a cup of water, a teaspoon and a half of palm oil. Everything goes into a cool, shallow, non-stick pan before any heat, which is the opposite of amala. Then it is stirred continuously on low-medium while the orange oil melds into the starch in swirls, and the endpoint is visual rather than timed — translucence, what the author calls glassy orange. Three quarters of a cup of water gives a softer result.
ingredients: 1/2 cup water, at room temperature — or 3/4 cup for a softer consistency
equipment: Cool, shallow non-stick frying pan — not a pot
steps: Combine the starch, water and palm oil in a cool, shallow non-stick frying pan.
Place the pan on low-medium heat and stir.
Monitor it as the mixture thickens and the orange palm oil colour melds into the starch in swirls.
Pull the cooked mass to the edge of the pan, using the pan side as a leveller.
Keep it free from lumps, scraping the edges against the pan sides.
Continue stirring until it achieves translucence and a glassy orange appearance.
If the bottom flakes too much, sprinkle in a touch of water. If the orange is too light, add palm oil drop by drop.
Serve immediately — a crisp film may form on the pan surface.
chefTips: Cool pan, cold start, everything in together. This is the opposite of amala (NGA001) where the flour goes into already-boiling water, and the two techniques are easy to confuse.
A shallow frying pan, not a pot. You need the pan wall to work against.
Pull the mass to the edge and use the side as a leveller. That is the specific move and it is how the lumps come out.
Translucence is the cue. The author's phrase is glassy orange, and the swirls go from distinct to blended as it gets there.
Water drop by drop if the bottom flakes; oil drop by drop if the colour is too pale. Small corrections only.
No time is given anywhere on the source page for any step — this runs entirely on the visual cue. Expect somewhere around ten to fifteen minutes on low-medium, but watch it rather than timing it.
Three quarters of a cup of water instead of half gives a softer starch. That is the author's own stated variation.
commonMistakes: Heating the pan before the ingredients go in.
Using a deep pot, so there is no wall to level against.
Stopping while it is still opaque.
Adding water by the spoonful rather than a sprinkle.
Letting it sit in the pan after it is done.
sources: Adapted from 'How to Make Starch, Usi', published on kitchenbutterfly.com. ATTRIBUTION: the byline prints as 'By Kitchen Butterfly', the site name, and not 'Ozoz Sokoh'; credited to the site accordingly. Published Aug 2, 2015, Modified June 3, 2026, the latter being part of a site-wide bulk stamp.

Quantities exactly as printed: 1 cup starch; 1/2 cup of water, room temperature; 1 & 1/2 teaspoons palm oil. Author's note as printed: 'If you want yours a bit softer, then go with 3/4 of a cup of water.' This is the most precisely specified recipe in any Nigerian source consulted.

The method and cues are as printed, including 'Pull the cooked mass to the edge using it as a leveller', 'If the bottom flakes too much, sprinkle a touch of water', 'If the orange is too light, add palm oil drop by drop', and the doneness description: 'The swirls become opaque, translucent, colours, light-absorbing abilities all blended', with the target 'translucence. Is the glassy orange.'
Yield as printed: one portion of firm starch; exact servings not specified.
Cultural note from the page, verbatim: 'Usi to my Isoko heritage. Of cassava, like corn starch.' Described as traditional to southern Nigeria.

GAP FLAGGED: no time is given for any step on the page. The whole method runs on visual cues, which leaves a first-time cook with no idea whether this is three minutes or fifteen. The estimate in the tips is labelled as an estimate.

A DISAGREEMENT ABOUT WHAT USI IS, not reconciled: the Itsekiri National Congress describes starch as 'a fermented cassava swallow that is unique to the Niger Delta', while the same site's cassava guide describes starch as a settled slurry — cassava peeled, washed, grated, left to settle so the thick starch slurry separates out, sold wet in blocks or dried — and does not list fermentation among its steps, though it does give fermentation times for garri, fufu and lafun. Whether usi is fermented is therefore genuinely open in the record.
A minor colour discrepancy within one site: the cassava guide calls cooked starch 'bright sunny yellow' while this recipe calls it 'glassy orange'.

A companion page, 'Sunday Lunch – Starch & Banga', carries NO ingredient list, no quantities and no yield at all — it is a memoir piece. Its usable contributions are the clay pot named Evwere, the reheating cue that banga is ready when 'a nice rim of dried palm nut cream forms', the trick of standing a saucer of water beneath the pot to prevent overheating, and the eating method: pinch a ball between thumb and forefinger, dip, swallow.
storage: Eat immediately. Starch does not keep or reheat well.
reheating: Not recommended. It goes hard and grainy.
healthBenefits: Cassava starch is easy to digest and gluten-free.
Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
Very low in fat for the amount of energy it provides.
culturalNote: Starch and banga is the Delta Sunday lunch, and the author's memoir piece describes first eating it as a child in Sunday best, with grandmother's fresh fish pepper soup thick with tilapia under the noon Isoko sun. It is eaten by pinching a ball between thumb and forefinger, dipping it in the soup and swallowing — and the pairing with banga is so fixed that one Itsekiri source says plainly that banga served with starch announces an Itsekiri table.
